1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Datasets.}
8	We evaluate on three English IE benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient.
9	\textbf{SciERC} \cite{luan2018scierc} contains 551 test instances annotated for joint NER (6 types) and RE (7 types).
10	\textbf{CoNLL-2003} \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} provides 3{,}453 test sentences with 4 entity types, where models achieve ${\approx}$91\% micro F1.
11	\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} consists of 1{,}287 social media instances with emerging entities, used to probe method boundaries (52\% zero F1).
12	
13	\paragraph{Models and sampling.}
14	Both \textbf{Qwen3-8B} and \textbf{LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct} are fine-tuned with LoRA (rank$=$32, $\alpha{=}64$) for 5 epochs using LLaMA Factory \cite{zheng2024llamafactory} under identical training procedures, ensuring comparisons across the two model families (both at 8B scale) reflect model differences rather than training confounds.
15	We note a training confound for SciERC: Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with \texttt{enable\_thinking=True} (LLaMA Factory 0.9.4 default), which prepends empty \texttt{<think>\textbackslash n</think>} blocks (4--5 tokens) to each training response and includes them in the loss computation; CoNLL-2003 and WNUT-17 checkpoints explicitly set \texttt{enable\_thinking=False}.
16	No reasoning content is present (the blocks are always empty), and constrained decoding at inference time enforces JSON-only output, so thinking tokens do not appear in generated samples.
17	This constitutes a minor train--test distribution mismatch for SciERC ($<$0.3\% of the 2048-token training window); CoNLL-2003 and WNUT-17 are unaffected.
18	We discuss implications in the Limitations section.
19	We draw $N{=}8$ samples at $T{=}1.0$ (primary; single seed, seed${=}42$), with $N{=}16$ for scaling experiments.\footnote{$N{=}16$ results for CoNLL (Qwen) and SciERC (LLaMA) are in Table~\ref{tab:robustness} (Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}); detailed $N$-scaling analysis in Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}. A 3-seed stability analysis ($\sigma{\leq}0.026$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}, Appendix~\ref{app:multiseed}) confirms that signal rankings are identical across seeds.}
20	Quality estimation uses Spearman $\rho$ and AUROC; downstream utility uses best-of-$N$ selection F1 with exact span matching (NER) and head-tail-label matching (RE).
21	Inference uses vLLM with constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}.
22	
23	%% ============================================================
24	\subsection{Quality Estimation Results}
25	\label{sec:qe_results}
26	
27	\begin{table*}[t]
28	\centering
29	\small
30	\caption{Quality estimation across tasks and models (Spearman $\rho$ and AUROC; $N{=}8$, seed${=}42$). Best value per column in \textbf{bold}. SciERC evaluates joint NER (6 types) and RE (7 types, single benchmark---preliminary); CoNLL evaluates NER (4 types). $N{=}16$ results appear in Table~\ref{tab:robustness} (Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).}
31	\label{tab:quality_estimation}
32	\begin{tabular}{ll cc cc cc cc}
33	\toprule
34	& & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{SciERC NER}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{SciERC RE}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{CoNLL (Qwen)}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{CoNLL (LLaMA)}} \\
35	\cmidrule(lr){3-4} \cmidrule(lr){5-6} \cmidrule(lr){7-8} \cmidrule(lr){9-10}
36	Signal & Family & $\rho$ & AUC & $\rho$ & AUC & $\rho$ & AUC & $\rho$ & AUC \\
37	\midrule
38	VC & Structural & \textbf{.379} & .684 & \textbf{.350} & .693 & .424 & .789 & .426 & .709 \\
39	SJ  & Structural & .360 & .692 & .250 & .670 & .436 & .801 & \textbf{.431} & .704 \\
40	FK & Surface & .267 & .629 & .275 & .609 & .400 & .774 & .428 & .703 \\
41	EM  & Surface    & .295 & \textbf{.749} & .134 & \textbf{.706} & \textbf{.451} & \textbf{.816} & \textbf{.431} & .705 \\
42	LP     & Model      & .205 & .578 & .266 & .600 & .316 & .753 & .307 & \textbf{.761} \\
43	\bottomrule
44	\end{tabular}
45	\end{table*}
46	
47	\begin{figure*}[t]
48	\centering
49	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_signal_heatmap}
50	\caption{Quality estimation heatmap (Spearman $\rho$) across five signals and four configurations. Left: full evaluation set; right: conditional set (non-zero F1 instances). On the full set, structural signals dominate on SciERC while all signals converge on CoNLL. On the conditional set, EM emerges as the strongest signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.360$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.417$), while LP RE collapses to near-zero ($\rho{=}0.011$).}
51	\label{fig:signal_heatmap}
52	\end{figure*}
53	
54	Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation} presents rank correlation ($\rho$) and AUROC for five confidence signals across tasks and models.
55	
56	\paragraph{Difficulty-dependent signal complementarity.}
57	On SciERC NER (complex schema, 6 types), structural signals lead: VC achieves $\rho{=}0.379$ and SJ $\rho{=}0.360$, both outperforming surface ($\rho{\leq}0.295$) and LP ($\rho{=}0.205$).
58	This advantage persists on RE (VC $\rho{=}0.350$; preliminary, single benchmark), though all signals weaken due to the 40\% zero-F1 floor effect.
59	VC and SJ show moderate instance-level correlation (NER: $\rho{=}0.659$; RE: $\rho{=}0.605$), indicating information overlap but not redundancy; their differential behavior across difficulty levels reflects the complementary granularity of entity-level frequency vs.\ span-level set overlap.
60	While the best $\rho{=}0.38$ (VC) explains approximately 14\% of F1 variance, the best AUROC reaches 0.749 (EM), indicating strong binary discriminative power for the quality/failure classification most relevant to practitioners in quality-aware routing.\footnote{Semantic entropy \cite{kuhn2023semantic} achieves comparable AUROC on discrete-answer QA; direct comparison is not meaningful due to different output spaces.}
61	Pairwise bootstrap CIs confirm the SJ advantage over LP ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.155$, CI excludes zero) but not over EM ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.065$, marginal under Bonferroni correction; Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap_signal_ci}, Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_signal}).
62	
63	\paragraph{$\rho$--AUROC dissociation.}
64	Signal choice depends on the intended use: on NER, EM leads AUROC (0.749) despite ranking third in $\rho$ (0.295), preferred for binary quality triage; structural signals ($\rho{\geq}0.36$) are better for fine-grained ranking.
65	On CoNLL with LLaMA, LP leads AUROC (0.761) yet trails in $\rho$ (0.307), confirming this pattern across datasets.
66	
67	\paragraph{Signal rankings shift with task difficulty.}
68	On CoNLL (greedy F1${\approx}$0.91), EM leads ($\rho{=}0.451$, AUROC${=}0.816$), surpassing SJ and VC.
69	When most samples are near-correct, binary agreement captures remaining variance more efficiently than set-level similarity.
70	This crossover---EM${>}$SJ on easy tasks vs.\ SJ${>}$EM on hard tasks---demonstrates difficulty-dependent complementarity rather than a universal structural advantage, suggesting practitioners should match signal type to expected task difficulty.
71	Stability across the two model families (both 8B) is strong: SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.436$ (Qwen) vs.\ $0.431$ (LLaMA) on CoNLL ($\Delta{=}0.005$, within 3-seed $\sigma{\approx}0.007$).
72	On WNUT-17, where 52\% of instances receive zero F1, full-set correlations are misleading: VC achieves $\rho{=}0.724$ (AUROC${=}0.913$), but this is entirely driven by the zero/non-zero boundary (conditional $\rho{=}0.038$, n.s.; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).
73	LP exhibits strong \textit{negative} correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$, AUROC${=}0.219$).
74	We hypothesize that this reversal reflects overconfidence on out-of-distribution inputs \citep{xiong2024llm}: the model assigns high log-probabilities to fluent but incorrect entity patterns (e.g., common noun phrases that resemble but do not match rare WNUT entity types), while producing lower scores for genuinely uncertain outputs where it correctly hedges.
75	On the conditional set, all signals collapse toward weak or non-significant correlations ($\rho{\leq}0.35$), with SJ achieving only $\rho{=}0.089$ ($p{=}0.020$) on the full set---suggesting a capability boundary beyond which consistency signals capture binary success/failure but not quality gradation.
76	
77	\paragraph{Conditional filtering.}
78	Filtering to non-zero F1 instances separates binary success detection (can the model extract \textit{anything}?) from quality gradation (among successful extractions, which are better?), but excludes the hardest instances where models fail completely---the conditional set is easier on average.
79	This reshuffles signal rankings (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}, right).
80	EM emerges as the strongest conditional signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.360$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.417$; preliminary), while VC and FK drop substantially (VC NER: $0.379{\to}0.300$; FK NER: $0.267{\to}0.176$).
81	LP RE collapses to $\rho{=}0.011$, confirming its full-set correlation was driven by zero/non-zero separation.
82	This creates a natural complementarity: VC and SJ are preferred on the full set, while EM provides the most precise ranking within the non-trivial subset (see Appendix~\ref{app:additional} for details).
83	
84	%% ============================================================
85	\subsection{The Correlation-Selection Gap}
86	\label{sec:selection_gap}
87	
88	\begin{figure*}[t]
89	\centering
90	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_selection_gap}
91	\caption{The correlation-selection gap on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Left: NER; right: RE. Bars show best-of-$N$ selection F1; the line marks quality estimation $\rho$. Despite $\rho$ up to 0.38, no signal significantly outperforms greedy on either task ($p{=}0.39$ for NER LP, the best signal; Table~\ref{tab:selection}). Dashed line indicates oracle upper bound.}
92	\label{fig:selection_gap}
93	\end{figure*}
94	
95	\begin{table}[t]
96	\centering
97	\small
98	\caption{Best-of-$N$ selection F1 on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). RE results are from a single benchmark (preliminary). Best non-oracle result per column in \textbf{bold}. Instance-level signals (SJ, FK, EM, VC) select the sample closest to the consensus output; VC uses majority-threshold voting ($>{N/2}$) for selection, distinct from the continuous QE score (Eq.~\ref{eq:voting}).}
99	\label{tab:selection}
100	\begin{tabular}{lcc}
101	\toprule
102	Method & NER F1 & RE F1 \\
103	\midrule
104	Oracle & 0.776 & 0.585 \\
105	\midrule
106	LP           & \textbf{0.650} & 0.395 \\
107	SJ       & 0.645 & 0.386 \\
108	EM        & 0.636 & 0.372 \\
109	VC                 & 0.634 & 0.359 \\
110	\midrule
111	Greedy ($T{=}0$)   & 0.644 & \textbf{0.404} \\
112	Random             & 0.608 & 0.354 \\
113	\bottomrule
114	\end{tabular}
115	\end{table}
116	
117	Despite strong quality estimation, confidence signals yield limited gains when used for best-of-$N$ selection (Table~\ref{tab:selection}, Figure~\ref{fig:selection_gap}).
118	Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input regardless of which sample is evaluated; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
119	The non-trivial question is whether log-probability---the only per-sample signal---can exploit the oracle headroom.
120	We anchor this analysis on SciERC, where output diversity is substantial: only 11--18\% of instances produce identical outputs across all $N{=}8$ samples, with 39--43\% unique outputs per instance (mean 3.5 distinct outputs), per-sample F1 standard deviation of 0.11--0.14, and mean pairwise SJ of 0.703.
121	
122	\paragraph{No significant improvement over greedy.}
123	We exclude 22 instances with empty gold annotations ($n{=}529$) and evaluate significance via instance-level paired bootstrap resampling ($B{=}10{,}000$).
124	On NER, the oracle (0.776) reveals 13.2~pp of headroom above greedy (0.644).
125	LP achieves the highest selection F1 (0.650, +0.6~pp), but this is not significant ($p{=}0.39$; 95\% CI: [$-$3.0, +4.2]~pp; Cohen's $d{=}0.038$).
126	On RE, the best signal (LP, 0.395) falls below greedy (0.404, $-0.9$\,pp, $p{=}0.80$), while 18.1~pp of oracle headroom remains; cross-seed analysis confirms RE LP failures are partially systematic (Appendix~\ref{app:lp_failure_stability}).
127	TOST equivalence testing confirms most signals are indistinguishable from greedy at ${\pm}2$--$3$~pp on NER; on RE, EM and VC fail equivalence even at ${\pm}5$~pp (Table~\ref{tab:tost}, Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}).
128	VC ($\rho{=}0.379$, the best quality estimator) selects to only 0.634 on NER---\textit{significantly below} greedy ($\Delta{=}{-}2.6$~pp, $p{<}0.03$ across 3 seeds).
129	The gap extends to CoNLL (ceiling effect, 57--88\% identical outputs) and WNUT-17 (capability boundary; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
130	
131	\paragraph{Quality estimation $\neq$ output selection.}
132	Instance-level confidence signals predict \textit{which inputs} the model handles reliably, not \textit{which output} among $N$ candidates is best.
133	When per-sample variance is low relative to instance-level difficulty, even perfect quality estimation cannot discriminate among near-identical candidates.
134	This gap has direct consequences for test-time scaling in IE \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}: closing it likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers}.
135	
136	%% ============================================================
137	\subsection{Robustness}
138	\label{sec:robustness_main}
139	
140	Consistency-based signals show robust performance across $T{\in}\{0.7, 1.0\}$ (SJ NER $\Delta\rho{=}0.028$, bootstrap CI includes zero) and sublinear gains from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, with structural signals maintaining their advantage over LP across all NER settings ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.135$ to ${+}0.175$; Table~\ref{tab:robustness}, Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).
141	On RE, only VC consistently outperforms LP ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.012$, preliminary).
142	NER signals are reasonably calibrated (ECE 0.069--0.096; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}), while RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339) and compound errors impose a ceiling at $\rho{\approx}0.28$ for $N{=}16$.

1	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
4	For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).
5	Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
6	At higher sample sizes ($N{=}16$), SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\Delta{=}0.002$) with lower cross-seed variance ($\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\ $0.026$); on RE, only VC consistently outperforms LP (preliminary).
7	When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).
8	
9	\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
10	\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
11	Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
12	\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.
13	LP scores are severely compressed: the median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats, below the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold at which 60\% of instances are effectively tied, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons fall within $|\Delta|{<}0.026$ (Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
14	In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
15	This diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression is the primary mechanistic bottleneck.
16	A controlled NER ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that LP compression persists without constrained decoding; on RE, the interaction is task-dependent.
17	Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.
18	
19	\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
20	Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
21	Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
22	\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.
23	
24	\paragraph{Score compression under free-form decoding.}\label{sec:ablation}
25	A natural hypothesis is that LP compression is an artifact of constrained decoding's restricted token space.
26	We test this via controlled ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, single dataset): generating free-form (unconstrained) outputs on the same instances with post-hoc JSON parsing (parse rate 99.95\%, 4406/4408; Table~\ref{tab:freeform_ablation}).
27	For NER, LP variance is essentially unchanged (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$, tied fraction 59.7\%$\to$57.7\%) and selection gains remain negligible ($+0.18$~pp free-form vs.\ $+0.59$~pp constrained), establishing that NER LP compression persists independent of decoding regime in our setting.
28	However, the ablation reveals a task-dependent interaction: RE LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single seed).
29	This reversal falls within the NER bootstrap 95\% CI [$-3.0$, $+4.2$]~pp and is based on a single seed, so we do not treat it as a confirmed finding; it suggests that constrained decoding may interact differently with RE but requires multi-seed replication.
30	The NER/RE divergence indicates that the relationship between decoding regime and selection is task-specific in our setting.
31	Notably, the fine-tuned model achieved 99.95\% parse rate without grammar constraints, suggesting that constrained decoding's format-compliance role may be redundant for sufficiently fine-tuned models.
32	
33	\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
34	The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
35	On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
36	The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
37	This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
38	This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
For per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
At higher sample sizes ($N{=}16$), SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\Delta{=}0.002$) with lower cross-seed variance ($\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\ $0.026$); on RE, only VC consistently outperforms LP (preliminary).
When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).

\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.
LP scores are severely compressed: the median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats, below the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold at which 60\% of instances are effectively tied, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons fall within $|\Delta|{<}0.026$ (Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
This diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression is the primary mechanistic bottleneck.
A controlled NER ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that LP compression persists without constrained decoding; on RE, the interaction is task-dependent.
Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\paragraph{Score compression under free-form decoding.}\label{sec:ablation}
A natural hypothesis is that LP compression is an artifact of constrained decoding's restricted token space.
We test this via controlled ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, single dataset): generating free-form (unconstrained) outputs on the same instances with post-hoc JSON parsing (parse rate 99.95\%, 4406/4408; Table~\ref{tab:freeform_ablation}).
For NER, LP variance is essentially unchanged (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$, tied fraction 59.7\%$\to$57.7\%) and selection gains remain negligible ($+0.18$~pp free-form vs.\ $+0.59$~pp constrained), establishing that NER LP compression persists independent of decoding regime in our setting.
However, the ablation reveals a task-dependent interaction: RE LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single seed).
This reversal falls within the NER bootstrap 95\% CI [$-3.0$, $+4.2$]~pp and is based on a single seed, so we do not treat it as a confirmed finding; it suggests that constrained decoding may interact differently with RE but requires multi-seed replication.
The NER/RE divergence indicates that the relationship between decoding regime and selection is task-specific in our setting.
Notably, the fine-tuned model achieved 99.95\% parse rate without grammar constraints, suggesting that constrained decoding's format-compliance role may be redundant for sufficiently fine-tuned models.

\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
Second, the non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible---score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
Effective selection likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.
Cross-dataset evaluation confirms that structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (VC $\rho{=}0.469$ OOD vs.\ $0.379$ in-domain); the reverse direction fails due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
Our findings are established under constrained decoding at 8B scale; a single-dataset NER ablation suggests LP compression persists without constrained decoding, but RE shows task-dependent interaction with decoding regime.
Whether these patterns generalize across datasets, model scales, and decoding strategies warrants further investigation.

\paragraph{Sample size scaling.}
Increasing from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ improves SJ on Qwen SciERC NER: $\rho$ rises from 0.360 to $0.411{\pm}0.010$ (three seeds: 0.398, 0.423, 0.410), a gain of $+0.047$.

FK $N$-scaling is inconsistent: degradation on SciERC ($-0.007$ to $-0.019$) but improvement on CoNLL with LLaMA ($+0.027$), suggesting sensitivity to both model and task characteristics.
VC $N$-scaling is consistently positive ($+0.005$ on Qwen CoNLL, $+0.018$ on LLaMA SciERC, $+0.030$ on Qwen SciERC), while LP is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta{\leq}0.034$).

On CoNLL, the gap across model families is minimal (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ (LLaMA) vs.\ 0.436 (Qwen), $\Delta{=}0.005$.
At $N{=}16$, the structural-over-LP advantage holds across all four tested NER settings: Qwen SciERC (VC $\rho{=}0.409$ vs.\ LP 0.239, $\Delta{=}{+}0.170$), Qwen CoNLL (EM $\rho{=}0.463$ vs.\ LP 0.328, $\Delta{=}{+}0.135$), LLaMA SciERC (VC $\rho{=}0.452$ vs.\ LP 0.277, $\Delta{=}{+}0.175$), and LLaMA CoNLL 3-seed (SJ $\rho{=}0.463{\pm}0.007$ vs.\ LP $0.310{\pm}0.005$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.153$).

\section{Additional Analyses}\label{app:additional}

\paragraph{Per-relation diagnostic.}
RE signal degradation is relation-specific.
\textsc{Feature-Of} has near-zero correlation ($\rho{=}0.004$), while \textsc{Hyponym-Of} achieves $\rho{=}0.646$.
The primary bottleneck is entity span errors, which account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives---a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect, as they measure agreement among equally incorrect extractions.
We note that RE analysis relies on a single dataset (SciERC); generalization to other RE benchmarks remains to be validated.

\paragraph{Capability stratification.}
For NER, SJ effectiveness scales with structural complexity: on SciERC instances with 6+ entities, $\rho{=}0.547$, compared to $\rho{=}0.415$ for 1--2 entities.
The SJ advantage over LP remains stable across sentence-length quartiles ($\Delta\rho{\approx}0.08$--$0.20$).
For RE, SJ $\rho$ increases monotonically with sentence length (Q1: 0.110 $\to$ Q4: 0.473; Fisher $z$-test $p{=}0.004$), indicating that longer, more relation-dense sentences provide richer structure for consistency-based estimation.
Both proxies are weakly correlated with F1 ($|r|{<}0.15$), confirming they capture input complexity rather than directly predicting output quality; however, entity count and sentence length are themselves moderately correlated ($\rho{=}0.650$), so they reflect overlapping rather than independent complexity dimensions.
For RE, entity count and relation count are strongly correlated ($\rho{=}0.769$) and thus reflect a single structural complexity dimension rather than independent axes.
On the high-complexity RE subset ($n{=}81$, high relation count), signals improve substantially: VC reaches $\rho{=}0.630$, LP $\rho{=}0.554$, and SJ $\rho{=}0.502$---all far above the full-set levels.
Richer relational structure provides more signal for consistency-based estimation, complementing the task-level boundary established by WNUT-17: structural signals are most effective within a ``sweet spot'' of sufficient model capability and sufficient output complexity.

\paragraph{Length vs.\ log-probability.}
Figure~\ref{fig:length_logprob_scatter} shows that mean log-probability is weakly positively correlated with output length (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$, $n{=}4{,}232$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$, $n{=}3{,}176$), ruling out length-penalty confounding as an explanation for LP's selection failure: longer outputs receive \textit{higher}, not lower, token-averaged log-probability under constrained decoding.

\label{fig:length_logprob_scatter}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evaluation circularity and LOO-SJ equivalence.}
Consensus-proximity selection chooses $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Leave-one-out SJ (LOO-SJ) for sample $y_i$ is $\text{LOO-SJ}_i = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Since the $\frac{1}{N-1}$ constant is shared across all candidates within an instance, $\arg\max_{y_i} \text{LOO-SJ}_i = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$, making the two selection rules equivalent.
Standard (non-LOO) SJ adds the self-comparison term $\text{SJ}(y_i, y_i) = 1$ to each candidate, which is constant and thus does not affect ranking.
Empirically, LOO-SJ yields $\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.014$ relative to standard SJ (a correlation-level difference), with a maximum per-instance score difference of $3.1{\times}10^{-4}$ (negligible at the individual prediction level).
Evaluation circularity is negligible.

\paragraph{Conditional filtering details.}
On LLaMA conditional RE (non-zero F1 instances), SJ recovers to $\rho{=}0.405$ while FK drops to $\rho{=}0.259$, confirming that structural advantage is robust across both models and evaluation conditions.
At $N{=}16$, the divergence persists: SJ maintains $\rho{=}0.308$ on conditional RE while LP drops to $\rho{=}{-}0.026$.
EM ranks first across all four tested conditional configurations---SciERC NER ($\rho{=}0.360$), CoNLL Qwen $N{=}16$ ($\rho{=}0.466$), CoNLL LLaMA 3-seed ($\rho{=}0.462$), and SciERC RE ($\rho{=}0.417$)---despite full-set rankings ranging from \#1 (CoNLL Qwen) to \#5 (SciERC RE).
On the full set, EM is diluted by trivial agreement: instances where all $N$ samples produce identical (possibly incorrect) outputs receive EM${=}1$ regardless of quality, compressing the signal's dynamic range.
On the conditional set---where the model demonstrably produces varied outputs---exact agreement becomes the strongest quality signal.
The margin over SJ is largest on RE ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.171$), where compound extraction decisions amplify output variability, and smallest on CoNLL LLaMA ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.002$), where all signals converge near $\rho{\approx}0.46$.

Table~\ref{tab:wnut} reports all five signals on WNUT-17.
VC achieves $\rho{=}0.724$ (AUROC${=}0.913$) on the full set, but conditional analysis (non-zero F1 instances) reveals this is entirely driven by the zero/non-zero boundary: conditional $\rho{=}0.038$ ($p{=}0.49$).
LP shows the reverse pattern: full-set $\rho{=}{-}0.410$ but conditional $\rho{=}0.350$, the highest among all signals on the conditional set.
This inversion confirms that full-set correlations on high-failure-rate datasets conflate binary success prediction with quality gradation.

\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}.
For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.047$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
Structural signals leverage $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, indicating diminishing information per additional comparison.
This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ LP $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.153$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while LP does not.
For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound---more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate---but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.

\paragraph{$N{=}16$ CoNLL selection: small but significant.}
While quality estimation benefits sublinearly from $N$-scaling, selection behavior at $N{=}16$ reveals a nuanced exception on LLaMA CoNLL.
VC achieves the largest gain over greedy ($+0.28$~pp, $p{=}0.003$--$0.027$ across 3 seeds, all significant), with SJ, FK, and EM at $+0.22$--$0.23$~pp and LP at $+0.12$~pp (2/3 seeds significant).
These gains are statistically significant but practically minimal: oracle headroom at $N{=}16$ is only 2.5~pp, so VC captures approximately 10\% of the available headroom.
This reinforces the core finding: even under the most favorable conditions---high baseline performance, more candidates, and aggregated multi-seed evidence---signal-based selection recovers only a fraction of the oracle headroom available.

\paragraph{Oracle-improvable fraction.}

\paragraph{Diversity-stratified selection gap.}
On the 44\% of Qwen SciERC instances with high diversity (${\geq}4$ unique outputs among 8 samples, $n{=}232$), oracle headroom reaches $+$16.3~pp, yet all consistency-based signals (SJ, FK, EM, VC) select at or below greedy, and LP---the only per-sample signal---achieves merely $+$0.8~pp.
LLaMA replicates this pattern: on its high-diversity subset ($n{=}186$), oracle headroom reaches $+$20.1~pp while consistency signals remain at or below greedy and LP captures only $+$2.0~pp.
This rules out insufficient diversity as an explanation for the correlation-selection gap.

\paragraph{TOST equivalence testing.}
The primary evidence against selection gains comes from effect sizes and confidence intervals: Cohen's $d{=}0.038$ for the best signal (NER LP) and bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$3.0, $+$4.2]~pp spanning zero.
Table~\ref{tab:tost} supplements this with two one-sided tests (TOST), testing whether each signal's selection F1 is equivalent to greedy within a bound $\delta$.
The $\delta$ values are anchored to oracle headroom (13--18~pp): $\delta{=}5$~pp corresponds to forgoing 28--38\% of the available headroom, $\delta{=}3$~pp forgoing 17--23\%, and $\delta{=}2$~pp less than 15\%.
The breakpoint $\delta^*$---the minimum equivalence margin at which each signal passes TOST---ranges from approximately 1.3~pp (SJ, ${\sim}$10\% of oracle headroom) to 3.4~pp (FK, ${\sim}$26\%) on NER, and from approximately 2.9~pp (LP, ${\sim}$16\%) to 6.5~pp (VC, ${\sim}$36\%) on RE.
On NER ($n{=}529$), at $\delta{=}{\pm}2$~pp, SJ and LP are confirmed equivalent to greedy (TOST $p{<}0.05$); at $\delta{=}{\pm}3$~pp, four of five signals pass; at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp, all five pass.
On RE ($n{=}397$, preliminary), EM and VC fail equivalence even at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp due to systematic underperformance ($\Delta{=}{-}3.2$~pp and $-4.5$~pp respectively).
The effect sizes are negligible ($d{=}0.038$) and confidence intervals span zero, with TOST confirming equivalence at practically meaningful margins.

\paragraph{Prompt template.}
For NER, we use a structured prompt:
\begin{quote}
\small
\texttt{System:} You are an expert in Named Entity Recognition.\\
\texttt{User:} Extract all named entities from the following text. Output as JSON.\\
Text: \texttt{\{input\_text\}}\\
Entity types: \texttt{\{schema\_types\}}
\end{quote}
RE follows the same structure with ``Relation Extraction'' and relation type lists substituted accordingly.

\paragraph{Constrained decoding.}
Inference uses vLLM with XGrammar-based JSON schema enforcement \cite{willard2023guided}, which constrains outputs to valid entity/relation structures matching the target schema.
This eliminates format errors but may compress per-sample diversity by restricting the output space.\footnote{SciERC training used \texttt{enable\_thinking=True} (LLaMA Factory 0.9.4 default), injecting empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks (4--5 tokens) into each training response with loss computation; CoNLL and WNUT explicitly set \texttt{enable\_thinking=False}. Constrained decoding at inference time enforces JSON-only output, suppressing thinking tokens. See \S\ref{sec:setup} and Limitations for discussion of this confound.}

\section{Log-Probability Score Compression}\label{app:logprob_ties}

Under constrained decoding, log-probability scores are severely compressed within instances, limiting per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}, Figure~\ref{fig:lp_range_cdf}).
The median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats---below the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold used throughout, providing data-driven justification for this cutoff rather than an arbitrary choice.
At $\varepsilon{=}0.05$, 60.3\% of instances ($n{=}529$, excluding empty gold annotations) have a within-sample range below the threshold, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$).
The CDF rises smoothly with no cliff or discontinuity (Figure~\ref{fig:lp_range_cdf}), confirming that compression is a pervasive regime rather than a bimodal split.
For comparison, SJ has only 12.5\% tied instances at the same threshold---SJ's advantage over LP for selection is one of score resolution, not information content.

\section{LP Selection Failure Stability}\label{app:lp_failure_stability}

We analyze RE LP selection failures across three random seeds (constrained decoding, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, Qwen3-8B) to assess whether failures are systematic or stochastic.

\paragraph{Pairwise overlap.}
LP selection failures (instances where LP-selected F1 $<$ greedy F1) show moderate cross-seed stability: the average pairwise Jaccard similarity is 0.42 (range: 0.38--0.46), indicating that failures are partially systematic---driven by instance complexity---but not fully deterministic.
The 3-way intersection contains 34 instances (27.9\% of any-seed failures), confirming a stable failure core.

\paragraph{Instance complexity drives failure.}
Table~\ref{tab:stable_failures} stratifies instances by failure stability.
Stable failures (all 3 seeds) involve more gold relations (2.12 vs.\ 1.62 for never-fail instances) and higher greedy F1 (0.688 vs.\ 0.429), indicating that LP mis-selects on instances where the model already performs well---precisely the instances where selection would be most valuable.
Failure rate increases monotonically with gold relation count: 4.3\% at 1 relation, 20.7\% at 3 relations, 26.2\% at 6 relations.
